overview: The JSON formatter validates JSON syntax, pretty-prints it with two-space indentation, or minifies it by removing all unnecessary whitespace. It is useful when an API response arrives as a single long line or when a configuration file needs to be checked before it is committed.

JSON is strict. A trailing comma, a missing quote, or a comment will cause a parse error. The tool reports the browser’s native error message so you can locate the problem quickly instead of guessing which line is wrong.
Everything runs in your browser. Large documents are limited only by available memory, and no data leaves the page.
useCases: Pretty-print a minified API response to read nested objects.
Minify a JSON configuration before embedding it in a URL or compact storage.
Validate a payload before sending it to an endpoint or saving it to a file.
Check that a hand-written JSON object is syntactically correct.
Prepare sample data for a test fixture or documentation example.
json-formatter.workedExample: Paste the compact string {"name":"Ada","scores":[98,91]}. Click Format. The output becomes a multi-line object with two-space indentation and the array on its own line. Click Minify to return to a single line with no extra spaces. If you remove the closing brace and click Validate, the tool shows an invalid JSON error instead of producing output.
limits: Only strict JSON is accepted. Comments, trailing commas and single quotes are rejected.
Very large documents may be slow to parse or may exceed the browser’s string size limits.
The error message comes from the browser’s JSON.parse implementation and may not include a line number in every browser.
Formatting uses two spaces; other indentation styles are not offered.
json-formatter.privacy: JSON is parsed and formatted entirely inside your browser. No document is uploaded, logged or stored.

faq.q: Why does a trailing comma fail?
faq.a: JSON does not allow trailing commas. The standard requires every value to be separated by a comma and the last item to have no trailing comma.

faq.q: Can I format JSON that contains comments?
faq.a: No. Comments are not part of JSON. Remove them before validating or use a JSONC-aware tool if you need comment support.

overview: The UUID generator creates version-4 UUIDs using the browser’s cryptographically secure random source when it is available. Version 4 identifiers are randomly generated and are the usual choice for database primary keys, correlation IDs and test data.
You can request from one to fifty values at a time. Each UUID is written on its own line so the list is easy to copy into a spreadsheet, a SQL insert or a JSON array.
The generator does not store the values it produces. Copy them before you leave the page if you need to keep them.
useCases: Create a primary key for a new database row.
Generate correlation IDs for distributed tracing or log aggregation.
Produce a batch of unique identifiers for test users or fixtures.
Obtain a quick unique token for a local prototype.
Fill a list of resource IDs for an API documentation example.
uuid-generator.workedExample: Set the count to 3 and click Generate. The output might look like 3f2504e0-4f89-11d3-9a0c-0305e82c3301 on the first line, followed by two more distinct values. Each string is 36 characters long, contains hyphens in the standard positions, and has the version digit 4 in the third group. Running the tool again produces an entirely new set.
limits: At most fifty UUIDs are generated in one click to keep the result readable.
Older browsers that lack the Web Crypto API fall back to Math.random, which is not suitable for security-sensitive tokens.
The tool does not check whether a generated UUID already exists in your database; uniqueness is probabilistic.
Version 1, 3, 5 and 7 UUIDs are not produced; only version 4 is available.
uuid-generator.privacy: Generation uses the browser’s random APIs and never sends the results anywhere. Nothing is stored after you close the page.

faq.a: Version 4 UUIDs are generated from random numbers. The version field is set to 4 and the variant bits follow the RFC 4122 layout.

faq.q: Are these safe for security tokens?
faq.a: They are suitable for ordinary application identifiers. For long-lived secrets or cryptographic keys, use a dedicated secret generator and a password manager.
